issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette:
Caleb Whitmore is a 32-year-old single white American man who has worked as a park ranger in a remote national forest in the Pacific Northwest for the past six years. He presented for psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 41, approximately fourteen months after an incident in which he was abducted and tortured by a group of individuals he encountered while conducting a routine patrol of a backcountry trail. The details of what happened over those hours remain fragmented even in his own telling - when he attempts to describe the event in session, he loses the thread of the narrative mid-sentence, falling silent and shaking his head as though the words have simply dissolved. Some moments are seared into him with almost unbearable clarity: the particular quality of the light through a stand of Douglas fir, the sound of a door being pulled shut and locked from the outside, the sensation of his wrists against restraints. Others are entirely blank - stretches of time he cannot account for, which disturb him perhaps more than the memories he does carry. He cannot, he says, really put any of it into words. It is less a story he can tell than something that lives in his body.

In the weeks following his rescue and medical discharge, Caleb returned to his apartment and largely did not leave it. His injuries had been assessed as serious but non-life-threatening, yet he had come to believe something more permanent had been done to him - that his body was fundamentally compromised in ways the doctors had either missed or not told him. He monitors physical sensations with vigilance, interpreting aches or fatigue as confirmation of lasting damage. When his hands trembled during a routine task, he was certain it was evidence of something neurological. What frightened him almost as much as this conviction was the speed of his own reactions: before he could form a conscious thought, his body would already be responding - heart slamming, muscles bracing - to a sound outside or a shadow crossing the window. He had begun to fear that this gap between stimulus and awareness meant something was fundamentally broken in his mind, that the reactions he could not control were signs he was losing his grip on sanity.

Caleb stopped driving entirely in the months after the event. He had been transported in a vehicle during the abduction, and the enclosed space of a car - the inability to exit, the sense of being moved without control - had become intolerable. This has had direct consequences for his work. Park rangers in his district are required to conduct vehicle patrols across large areas of terrain, and his inability to drive or ride as a passenger has meant he has been placed on indefinite administrative reassignment, a situation that has deepened his isolation from colleagues and from the landscape that once gave his life structure and meaning. Before any interaction with his supervisor or the HR office, he rehearses the conversation at length - running through possible exchanges, preparing responses - because he had come to believe that other people could not be relied upon to behave predictably or safely, and that preparation was the only protection available to him. He checks the locks on his doors and windows multiple times each evening, and when a delivery is late or a message goes unanswered longer than he expects, he assumes something bad is unfolding - that the delay is not ordinary but ominous. He has described numbing his feelings as something he does deliberately, as a kind of management, though he acknowledges that what he is left with most of the time is a flat, exhausted distance from everything.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a conversation with his younger sister, who had driven four hours to visit him and found the apartment darkened, the locks checked, and her brother unable to explain to her what had happened or why he was living this way. He agreed to an intake appointment, though he came with considerable ambivalence. He is most afraid, he said quietly at the end of the first session, that the person he was before is simply gone. What he is hoping for, with something that looked like careful restraint, is to be told that is not true.
